Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the injury pattern of upper and lower motor neurons relative to the location of the
cervical spinal cord injury.
Recognize the rationale for upper extremity reconstruction techniques in patients with
tetraplegia.
Describe common nerve and tendon transfers to restore elbow extension, grasp, and pinch.
Describe the pathophysiology of spasticity in patients with brain injury.
Discuss nonsurgical treatment options to alleviate pain, correct deformity, and enhance
function in patients with a brain injury and a spastic upper limb.
Explain the surgical treatment options to optimize function, improve hygiene, and improve
cosmesis in patients with a brain injury who have upper limb spasticity and contractures.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
An injury to the spinal cord consists of a combination of upper and lower motor neuron
injuries.
Tetraplegia or quadriplegia refers to paralysis that results in partial or complete loss of motor
and sensory function within all four extremities because of a cervical spinal cord injury (SCI).

Overview
A SCI can result in partial or complete loss of motor function and sensibility of all four
extremities, otherwise known as tetraplegia. Loss of upper extremity function may
markedly decrease a patient’s function, independence, and quality of life. Approximately
49% of patients with tetraplegia state that recovery or restoration of upper extremity
function is their highest priority. Similarly, approximately 77% of patients with tetraplegia
believe that improved hand function would result in marked enhancement to their
quality of life.
Epidemiology
An estimated 10 to 80 new cases of SCI per million annually
The cervical spine is injured in approximately 50% of patients, which leads to tetraplegia.
Although 65% of patients with tetraplegia are candidates for upper extremity reconstructive
surgery, fewer than 400 surgical procedures for the management of tetraplegia are performed
annually.

Epidemiology
Although many patients with tetraplegia are candidates for upper extremity
reconstruction, only a small percentage of patients undergo surgical treatment. This
disparity is multifactorial and may be, in part, attributed to a lack of awareness of by
physiatrists and therapists of surgical procedures to reanimate the upper extremity,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
2/36

limited patient access to surgeons who perform these unique surgeries, and
apprehension of patients to undergo a reconstructive procedure that may restrict their
activities for a short period of time or hinder their independence during the
rehabilitation phase.
Neuroanatomy
Neuroanatomy1,2,3
(Resources 1, 2, 3)
Upper motor neurons (UMNs) consist of the cell bodies that reside in the brain and course
through the spinal cord.
Lower motor neurons (LMNs) consist of the cell bodies that originate in the anterior horn
within the spinal cord.
UMNs create a synaptic connection with LMNs within the spinal cord to transmit motor
impulses.

Neuroanatomy
Each spinal cord level consists of traversing UMNs and exiting LMNs. Deficits after SCI
are to the result of UMN and LMN injuries at a particular level. Therefore, consideration
of the UMNs and LMNs with respect to their position relative to the level of injury is
useful: supralesional, intralesional, and infralesional (Figure 1).
Supralesional axons, both UMNs and LMNs, remain uninjured and function properly.
Intralesional nerves include UMNs traversing through the zone of injury to a caudal site
of nerve synapse and LMNs exiting at the level of injury. Infralesional nerves include
intact and uninjured LMNs yet without innervation because of injured UMNs.
The distinction between UMNs and LMNs becomes critical in considering their respective
contributions to extremity function and differential responses to injury. Intralesional
LMN injuries in particular may impart a temporal sensitivity given that the muscles they
innervate are susceptible to irreversible atrophy and fibrosis with loss of motor end
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
3/36

plates after approximately 12 months of denervation. Infralesional LMNs continue to
provide trophic innervation to their associated skeletal muscles indefinitely, removing
any time constraints from future surgical management. This renders infralesional LMNs
and their associated muscles useful as nerve transfer recipients or as potential
functional free muscle transfer donors.
Figure 1
Sagittal MRI of a spine with a complete spinal cord injury at C3-C4 shows upper motor
nerve and lower motor nerve injury at various levels. The supralesional levels have
uninjured upper and lower motor nerves (green shaded box). The intralesional levels
have injured upper and lower motor nerves (red shaded box). The infralesional levels
have injured upper motor nerves and uninjured lower motor nerves (blue shaded box).
(Reproduced with permission from Cantwell SR, Rhee PC: Upper-extremity
reconstruction in tetraplegia: A critical analysis review. JBJS Rev 2020;8[7]:e1900210.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Strength is assessed using the Medical Research Council system.
Passive joint range of motion (ROM) is noted to evaluate for soft-tissue contractures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
4/36

The presence of underlying spasticity, a heightened motor response as a result of a rapid
stretch, is determined.

Physical Examination
Evaluation of the upper extremity in patients with tetraplegia should focus on active
and/or passive ROM of the elbow, wrist, fingers, and thumb. Limitations in passive ROM
may be secondary to internal joint derangement, myostatic or joint contractures,
heterotopic ossification, skeletal malalignment, or spasticity. In addition, the motor
strength of all muscles in the upper extremity should be documented using the Medical
Research Council system to determine if any neuromotor units may serve as suitable
donors for nerve or tendon transfers (Table 1).

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Prevention of contractures and maintenance of ROM should begin as soon as possible after
the SCI.
Maintaining skin integrity is crucial to the treatment of patients with an SCI.

Nonsurgical Management
Stretching of the muscles to prevent myostatic contractures and passive motion to
maintain physiologic ROM should be initiated immediately. Orthoses that place the wrist
in extension, the fingers in slight flexion, and the thumb in an abducted position are
beneficial to prevent the development of a clenched fist or thumb-in-palm deformity
while permitting hygiene and care to the palm of the hand. Functional electrical
stimulation can be used to stimulate muscle contractions that may preserve muscle
bulk, enhance muscle control, and even decrease muscle spasms.
Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical treatment may be considered in patients who have reached a plateau in neuromotor
function improvement based on serial physical examinations after a reasonable amount of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
7/36

time that would be expected for neurorecovery.
Psychologic and socioeconomic stability are necessary to ensure that the patient can endure
the stressors of reconstructive surgery and subsequent rehabilitation.
All medical comorbidities must be optimized preoperatively to minimize the risk of
perioperative complications.

Indications
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients in whom neurorecovery has plateaued on
serial physical examinations after a reasonable amount of time that would be expected
for return of nerve function. Patients with neurologic injuries, especially those with
incomplete injuries, often demonstrate some degree of neurorecovery without surgical
treatment. A plateau in neurorecovery may be achieved in 6 months in patients with
complete tetraplegia, permitting earlier surgical treatment and earlier subsequent
functionality; however, a minimum of 9 to 12 months of observation ensures no further
meaningful neurorecovery can occur.
Most importantly, patients must demonstrate psychologic stability, possess adequate
social support, and achieve optimization of medical comorbidities to minimize the risk of
perioperative complications and ensure that they can participate in postoperative
rehabilitation and adhere to any postoperative restrictions.
Goals of Management
The goals of upper extremity reconstructive surgery in patients with tetraplegia include
improving function and enhancing quality of life.
Restoring active elbow extension enables the patient to place the hand out in space.
Restoration of active or passive grasp and pinch may markedly improve the performance of
basic tasks and activities of daily living.
In patients with a low cervical SCI, restoration of finger release, intrinsic function, and thumb
opposition may be possible.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
8/36


Goals of Management
The goals of management include minimizing pain, improving function, increasing
independence, and enhancing quality of life. Surgical procedures are directed at
achieving active elbow extension and restoring active or passive grasp and pinch. The
ability to actively extend the elbow, allowing the hand to travel an additional 12 inches in
space, increases the workspace of the hand by 800%. Similarly, restoring grasp and
pinch in a paralyzed hand may permit the patient to hold a utensil to feed themselves,
operate a cellphone or tablet, or steer a motorized wheelchair. In patients with a low
cervical SCI, additional reconstructive options may exist to enhance hand function,
specifically with reanimation of finger release, intrinsic function, or thumb opposition.
Techniques/Procedures
Tendon transfers typically are used to restore elbow extension, grasp, and pinch.
Nerve transfers are an innovative method to transfer healthy axons to injured LMNs to
reinnervate paralyzed muscles.
Adjunctive procedures often are necessary to enhance the performance of tendon or nerve
transfers.

Techniques/Procedures
Tendon transfers offer a predictable and reliable means to restore the critical functions
of active elbow extension and active or passive grasps and pinch. Given that joints
remain supple and donor muscles stay sufficiently strong, tendon transfers can be
performed decades after SCI. The same prerequisites for tendon transfer in the non-
tetraplegic population apply to tetraplegia reconstruction, which include having supple
joints; volitional muscle control; strength of at least M4 (expect a decrease of at least one
grade with transfer); adequate tendon excursion; action across a single joint; and,
ideally, function synergistic with the native function of the musculotendinous unit.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
9/36

Nerve transfers have emerged as a supplement and a substitute for traditional tendon
transfer procedures in patients with tetraplegia. Supralesional LMNs can serve as donors
to injured intralesional LMNs or uninjured infralesional LMNs that lack UMN control.
Nerve transfers also may fill a therapeutic gap, providing additional options to patients
in low ICSHT groups who have limited tendon transfer options or patients in whom the
tendon of an intact neuromotor unit cannot function as a reliable donor because of a
mismatch in tendon/muscle excursion and strength for the function that is attempting to
be restored.
Lastly, adjunctive procedures often are necessary to optimize the performance of
tendon and nerve transfers to restore grasp and pinch. Such procedures include
selective joint arthrodesis to provide a secure platform for thumb function and tendon
shortening or stabilization procedures to correct tendon imbalances across a joint.
Restoration of Elbow Extension4,5,6
(Resources 4, 5, 6)
Tendon transfers are effective at restoring anti-gravity elbow extension in patients with
tetraplegia.
The posterior deltoid or biceps can be transferred to the distal triceps to power elbow
extension.
Nerve transfers are emerging as a possible alternative to reinnervate the paralyzed triceps
muscles.

Restoration of Elbow Extension
Elbow extension can be restored via transfer of the posterior deltoid or the biceps to the
triceps tendon and/or the olecranon. The posterior deltoid transfer requires a tendon
graft to extend the posterior deltoid to the triceps insertion. Autogenous free tendon
grafts that have been used include the tibialis anterior, fascia lata, central one-third of
the triceps tendon, hamstring, and toe extensor tendon, as well as various synthetic
materials. Although the posterior deltoid-to-triceps transfer has been extensively used to
restore elbow extension, the technique remains limited by the need for tendon
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
10/36

interposition grafting, suboptimal excursion of the posterior deltoid to fully restore
elbow extension, arduous postoperative immobilization requirements, and the risk for
tendon attenuation with time.
The biceps-to-triceps tendon transfer is a suitable alternative to restore active elbow
extension. Although initial concerns existed with regard to donor site morbidity, non-
synergism, and risk of damage to the radial nerve with lateral routing of the biceps
tendon en route to the triceps, these have been disproven or circumvented via
procedural modifications. The biceps-to-triceps transfer is a viable option in patients
with muscle redundancy to perform elbow flexion (brachialis and/or brachioradialis
[BCR] intact) and supination (supinator intact). The distal biceps tendon has adequate
excursion and length to permit a solid insertion into a bone tunnel within the olecranon
that often is woven through the distal triceps to augment the strength of attachment.
Nerve transfers to restore elbow extension bypass several drawbacks associated with
tendon transfers and provide reasonable functional outcomes. Donor nerves include the
motor branch to the teres minor, posterior deltoid, or brachialis transferred to the
motor branch of the long or medial head of the triceps. Although small case series and
anatomic feasibility studies have been reported, additional clinical studies are necessary
to determine the role of nerve transfers compared with tendon transfers to regain elbow
extension.
Restoration of Grasp4,5,6
Grasp can be restored with tendon or nerve transfers to the extrinsic finger flexors within the
forearm.
Active grasp is achieved if a donor nerve or muscle powers extrinsic finger flexor tendon
excursion independent of wrist position.
Passive grasp relies on active wrist extension to produce reciprocal finger flexion because of
the tenodesis effect.
Grasp release can be optimized via extrinsic finger extensor tenodesis to the distal radius or
restored via nerve transfer to the posterior interosseous nerve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
11/36


Restoration of Grasp
Active or passive grasp can be restored via tendon transfers. In patients with a high
cervical SCI (ICHST group1), the BCR tendon can be transferred to the extensor carpi
radialis brevis to reinstate passive grasp through active wrist extension with reciprocal
finger flexion via the tenodesis effect. However, in patients with preserved function in
the radial wrist extensors, extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi radialis
brevis, active grasp can be achieved via transfer of the extensor carpi radialis longus to
the flexor digitorum profundus tendons of the index through little fingers. Because of
the intrinsic minus deformity in most patients with tetraplegia, intrinsic tendon function
can be restored via tendon transfer or tendon reconstruction to create a more
physiologically natural embrace-grasp-release process.
Nerve transfers present another innovative option to restore grasp in patients with a
high cervical SCI in whom suitable donor muscles are not available for tendon transfers.
For patients in ICSHT group 0, the brachialis motor branch can be transferred to the
extensor carpi radialis longus motor branch to establish passive grasp. Alternatively, the
brachialis motor branch can be transferred to the anterior interosseous nerve or to the
median nerve fascicles that innervate the wrist, finger, and/or thumb flexors (eg, flexor
digitorum profundus, flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor pollicis longus, or flexor carpi
radialis). Even transfer of the entire musculocutaneous nerve to the median nerve has
been described to reinnervate the finger flexors for active grasp. Additional clinical
studies are necessary to determine the role of nerve transfers versus tendon transfers
for grasp restoration in patients with tetraplegia.
The ability to grasp objects can be enhanced by facilitating active or passive finger
extension that enables the acquisition of larger objects into the hand and the release of
held objects. Patients who can perform active wrist extension (ICSHT groups 2 through 4)
can utilize the tenodesis effect to open the hand for release or in preparation for grasp.
Passive release can be enhanced via tenodesis of the extensor digitorum communis
tendons under tension to the dorsal distal radius. In patients with an intact biceps and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
12/36

supinator motor function, transfer of the supinator motor branch to the posterior
interosseous nerve can be performed to restore active finger and thumb extension.
Restoration of Pinch4,5,6
Active or passive pinch can be restored via tendon transfers.
If active wrist extension is present, the BCR can be transferred to the flexor pollicis longus to
restore active pinch.
If no suitable donor tendons are available for transfer to the flexor pollicis longus, passive
pinch can be performed with use of the tenodesis effect and enhanced via flexor pollicis
longus tenodesis to the distal radius under tension.
Because of the lack of thenar muscles, restoration of trapeziometacarpal joint stability via
arthrodesis or opposition transfer may be helpful if donor muscles are available.

Restoration of Pinch
Active or passive appositional or key pinch can be restored via tendon transfers. Donor
tendons to support active pinch include the BCR or pronator teres, which can be
transferred to the flexor pollicis longus. The BCR can only be used as a donor tendon if
active wrist extension is present. If active wrist extension is absent, the BCR is better
suited for transfer to the extensor carpi radialis brevis to accommodate passive grasp
and pinch via the tenodesis effect. However, in this situation, passive pinch can be
enhanced via tenodesis of the flexor pollicis longus to the volar distal radius under
tension.
Additional procedures can be performed to further optimize active or passive pinch. In
most patients, the thenar muscles are paralyzed, thus creating instability at the first
carpometacarpal joint. Stability to the thumb carpometacarpal joint can be afforded via
arthrodesis or opposition transfer based on the level of cervical SCI and the availability
of donor muscles/tendons to power opposition. Similarly, the thumb interphalangeal
joint can be stabilized via an extensor loop knot or split flexor pollicis longus to extensor
pollicis longus transfer to prevent hyperflexion at the interphalangeal joint during pinch
because of the absence of extensor pollicis longus function. Lastly, pinch release can be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
13/36

enhanced via tenodesis of the extensor pollicis longus to the dorsal distal radius under
tension.
Postoperative Management/Rehabilitation
Active and passive ROM is encouraged a few days after upper extremity reconstruction for
tetraplegia.
Tendon repair and joint arthrodesis constructs should be strong enough to withstand early
ROM.
In patients who undergo nerve transfers, the upper extremity is protected for 3 weeks to
prevent nerve coaptation rupture.

Postoperative Management/Rehabilitation
In most patients, early active and passive ROM is initiated at 5 to 7 days after upper
extremity reconstruction for tetraplegia. If tendon transfers have been performed to
restore elbow extension, grasp, and pinch, the transfers are protected in an orthosis
while permitting supervised passive and active-assisted ROM to minimize the
development of joint contractures and tendon adhesions. Therefore, tendon repair
constructs should be strong enough to withstand the stresses that may be imparted to
the tendon transfers with early muscle activation and retraining. Similarly, if arthrodesis
has been performed, fixation technique should be strong enough to permit early active
and passive ROM; however, if nerve transfers have been performed, the upper extremity
is protected for 3 weeks to mitigate the occurrence of nerve coaptation failure.
Brain Injury
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview7,8
(Resources 7 and 8)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
14/36

A brain injury, whether acquired or congenital, may result in an injury to the cell bodies of
UMNs.
UMN syndrome is a constellation of dysfunction in motor function, control, and tone.

Overview
A central nervous system injury may result in decreased motor control, motor weakness,
easy fatigability, altered muscle tone, and/or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, which is
termed UMN syndrome. Initially, after an injury to the UMN, an immediate period of
flaccid paralysis (-plegia) or profound motor weakness (-paresis) ensues and may be
followed by a progressive increase in motor activation and tone (hypertonia). The altered
regulation of muscle control and/or loss of voluntary motor activity leads to unbalanced
forces across a joint, which may lead to dynamic or static postural deformities. UMN
syndrome may occur after a traumatic brain injury, cerebrovascular accident, anoxic
brain injury, cerebral palsy, or SCI.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Nerves
Injured UMNs result in hyperexcitable or exaggerated spinal reflexes, termed spasticity.

Nerves
UMNs transmit signals to the cell bodies of LMNs within the spinal cord. An injury to the
UMN results in the loss of inhibitory pathways and altered processing of intraspinal
primary afferent signals, which leads to hyperexcitable or exaggerated spinal reflexes.
Hyperreflexia may lead to increased muscle tone with amplified muscle activation in
response to a quick or slow stretch stimulus, termed spasticity or rigidity, respectively.
With prolonged and sustained muscle hypertonia, myostatic and joint contractures can
develop.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
15/36

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Assessment of volitional muscle control is critical in the management of spasticity, myostatic
contracture, or joint contracture.
Spasticity is evaluated by detecting abnormal motor tone or activation with a quick stretch (<1
second) of a muscle.

Physical Examination
The initial evaluation should focus on the resting posture of the upper extremity and a
thorough inspection of vulnerable areas for skin breakdown or poor hygiene secondary
to abnormal joint postures, particularly within the axilla, antecubital fossa, wrist flexion
crease, and palm. Active joint ROM is assessed to determine if volitional muscle control
is present and to grade the strength of muscle contraction.
Passive joint motion is appraised to determine the physiologic arc of motion of each
joint. Limitation in passive arc of motion may indicate the presence of soft-tissue
contractures from the muscles, ligaments, or joint capsule. In addition, passive ROM of
each joint in the upper extremity through its full arc of physiologic motion slowly (>1
second) or quickly (<1 second) is performed to detect the presence of rigidity or
spasticity, respectively. Co-contraction or inappropriate firing of an antagonist muscle
during the same phase as an agonist also is known as dyssynergy. Spasticity is classified
based on the Modified Ashworth Spasticity Score (Table 3).

Selective Neuromotor Blockade7,8
Selective peripheral nerve local anesthetic blockade can be used to determine if the motor
dysfunction is the result of spasticity rather than a muscle or joint contracture.

Selective Neuromotor Blockade
Local anesthesia can be used to selectively block neuromotor units to enhance the
evaluation of a patient with UMN syndrome. Because spasticity is neurally mediated,
temporary neuromuscular blockade with injection of a local anesthetic near the
innervating nerve may reduce or even eliminate pathologic motor tone. Therefore,
selective neuromotor blockade may be extremely beneficial to differentiate muscle
spasticity from soft-tissue or joint contractures. For example, injection of local anesthetic
to the musculocutaneous nerve that resolves the joint deformity may be attributed to
spasticity within the biceps and/or brachialis muscles; however, if the joint deformity
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
17/36

persists despite local anesthetic block, a muscle and/or joint contracture may be
present.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs of the upper extremity are performed to evaluate for fractures, joint
derangement, skeletal malalignment, and/or heterotopic ossification.

Radiography
Imaging studies of the upper extremity are performed to determine if a skeletal basis
exists for any deformities or limitations in joint motion, such as congenital dysplasia,
malalignment from a fracture, or degenerative versus posttraumatic arthritis. Because
traumatic brain injuries often are associated with the development of heterotopic
ossification, radiographs of the involved joints are necessary to determine if mechanical
block to motion exists.
Dynamic Electromyography7,8
Dynamic electromyography can be used to characterize motor activation patterns, detect
spasticity, and to identify volitional muscle control in the upper limb of patients with UMN
syndrome.

Dynamic Electromyography
Electromyography recordings are obtained with surface or fine-wire electrodes placed
onto or into target muscles during passive and active joint motion. Joint position tracings
with the use of a goniometer or via three-dimensional motion analysis can be obtained
to correlated electromyographic data with upper extremity kinematics, otherwise known
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:48 AM
AAOS | Tetraplegia and Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000558
18/36

as dynamic electromyography. Dynamic electromyography analysis can be used to
determine if volitional motor activation is present within a specific muscle and to identify
if the inability to perform full active motion is to the result of motor weakness or the
result of dyssynergy, which is an abnormal co-contraction of the antagonist muscles
during the same muscle firing phase as an agonist muscle.
Diagnosis
Surgeons must determine if abnormal joint posturing and limitation of motion is to the result
of rigidity, spasticity, dyssynergy, or soft-tissue contractures.
The absence or presence of volitional muscle control dictates the best form of management
for upper extremity deformities in patients with UMN syndrome.

Diagnosis
Upper extremity deformities in patients with UMN syndrome may be multifactorial,
highlighting the importance of a thorough physical examination with the use of adjuncts
for diagnosis, such as dynamic electromyography or selective local anesthetic nerve
blocks, to determine underlying or coexisting pathologic conditions. For example,
dysfunction within the agonist neuromotor units may be to the result of spasticity and/or
muscle contracture, yet the overall joint deformity may be exacerbated by periarticular
soft-tissue contractures and/or weakness, paralysis, or dyssynergy. Identifying all the
components to the joint deformity and dysfunction is critical so that the proper
treatment options can be used to manage each pathologic neuromotor unit.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management should be instituted with the goals of reducing spasticity,
maintaining passive ROM, preventing contractures, and decreasing pain.


Nonsurgical Management
The preferred treatment options for the nonsurgical management of UMN syndrome
include orthoses, physical therapy, pharmacologic agents, and functional electrical
stimulation.
Pharmacologic Agents
Antispasmodic agents can be ingested, infused into the thecal sac, or injected into muscles.
Botulinum toxin type A is commonly injected into spastic muscles to produce a neuromuscular
blockade.

Pharmacologic Agents
Pharmacologic agents (oral, intrathecal, or injectable) may decrease pain and improve
basic upper limb function. Typical oral medications used for patients with UMN
syndrome include anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antispasmodic agents. Although the
former two classes of medications may decrease pain, antispasmodic agents also may
improve function by reducing muscle spasticity. The mechanism of action for
antispasmotic agents include centrally acting medications (baclofen, tizanidine,
benzodiazepines, clonidine), inhibitors of calcium release within the sarcoplasmic
reticulum (dantrolene), and decreasing cholinergic activity at the neuromuscular junction
(botulinum toxin). Botulinum toxin type A is commonly injected into spastic muscles that
inhibit the presynaptic release of acetylcholine, exerting a blockade at the
neuromuscular junction.
Orthotics
Orthoses are beneficial in preventing progressive contractures and maintaining the extremity
in a functional position while facilitating hygiene.
Patient compliance is integral to enhance the efficacy of orthotic use.


Orthotics
The use of orthoses to prevent upper extremity contractures is integral to the early
rehabilitative program. Static resting splints are commonly used in patients without
volitional muscle activity to position the wrist and fingers in a functional and safe
position. Controversy exists regarding the positioning of the orthosis within the palmar
or dorsal surface of the hand in patients with spasticity. Although a palmar-based resting
splint can be applied in a patient with a flaccid upper extremity, it is postulated that a
dorsal-based orthosis should be used in patients with a spastic upper extremity because
the palmar contact may elicit a grasp reflex and may result in increased contact pressure
and promote the development of ulcers. Regardless, patient compliance is the most
important factor in the success of orthotic use in the upper extremity to prevent
contractures.
Physical Therapy
Stretching and motor retraining are the best treatment options to prevent contractures and
potentially restore functional movement, respectively.

Physical Therapy
Maintenance of upper extremity ROM via physical therapy is an integral modality for
nonsurgical management of UMN syndrome, specifically stretching. A routine physical
therapy regimen consists of motor retraining, if volitional motor control is present, and
muscle stretching that can be combined with daytime and/or nighttime orthotic use.
Stretching is performed to prevent muscle and joint contractures and can be facilitated
via antispasmodic agents if spasticity is present. In addition, functional electrical
stimulation can be used to increase activity of the cerebral sensory-motor cortex in
patients with a brain injury and may enhance the restoration of functional movement
and encourage firing of muscles in the correct phase of joint movement.

Surgical Management7,8,9,10
(Resources 9 and 10)
The goals of surgical management are to decrease pain, enhance function, and/or improve
quality of life.
Surgical treatment options are based on the potential for function as determined by the
presence of volitional motor control and intact sensibility.

Surgical Management
The primary goals of surgical treatment in patients with UMN syndrome are to reduce
pain, improve hygiene, enhance function, and/or correct unaesthetic contractures that
impair function. The goals of surgical management are based on the potential for
function within the upper extremity.
Surgical candidates can be classified as those with the possibility for a functional upper
extremity or are deemed to be nonfunctional. A nonfunctional hand has no volitional
motor control and no intact sensation. A potentially functional hand has volitional motor
control of individual joints and intact sensibility to gross touch. Many patients with UMN
syndrome will exhibit a mixed potential for function in the upper limb with volitional
control in one joint with an adjacent joint that may not be capable of any motor function.
Indications
Surgical treatment for patients with UMN syndrome should be delayed until a reasonable
amount of time has passed to ensure that neurologic recovery has plateaued.
A patient’s psychologic, emotional, and cognitive status must be evaluated to ensure no
barriers exist to obtaining consent, abiding by postoperative restrictions, and participating in
rehabilitation.
All medical comorbidities must be optimized before performing upper extremity
reconstructive surgery for the management of spasticity.

Indications
Surgical treatment should only be considered after a patient’s maximal expected
neurologic recovery has been reached. After a cerebrovascular accident or anoxic brain
injury, neurorecovery may begin to plateau within 6 months postinjury but may steadily
improve up to 12 months postinjury. After a traumatic brain injury, restoration of
neurologic function may peak within 12 to 18 months postinjury. Surgical management
should be withheld until no additional evidence of neurologic recovery is noted via serial
physical examinations. Therefore, surgical management typically can be performed as
early as 12 months after a cerebrovascular accident or cerebrovascular accident and at
least by 18 months after a traumatic brain injury.
To ensure that a patient is a suitable candidate for surgical treatment, the psychologic,
emotional, and cognitive status of the patient must be assessed to determine if any
impediments to the postoperative rehabilitation process exist. Damage to various areas
of the brain may result in an inability to communicate (expressive aphasia), understand
(receptive aphasia), or perform a previously learned action or task (apraxia). Although
these entities, if present, are not a contraindication to surgical treatment, special
consideration must be taken so that patients can communicate effectively with care
providers, are well-informed regarding the proposed surgical procedure and expected
outcomes, and can participate in rehabilitation and abide by postoperative restrictions.
Many patients have guardianships or medical decision makers who assist with or make
medical decisions on behalf of the patient. Clear expectations about the role of surgical
treatment, rehabilitation, risks, potential advantages, and expected outcomes should be
discussed with the patient and family, which often requires several visits with serial
discussions and ensuring that the entire care team is committed to realistic expectations
regarding the anticipated possible results of surgical treatment.
Preoperatively, any medical comorbidities must be optimized to decrease the risk of
perioperative complications. No active or ongoing infections may be present, especially
in intertriginous areas.

Overview of Techniques
Surgical procedures for upper extremity deformities and dysfunction in UMN syndrome must
be individualized.
Surgical techniques can be directed at specific targets within the dysfunctional neuromotor
unit, such as at the nerve, muscle origin, muscle belly, musculotendinous junction, or tendon.

Overview of Techniques
The surgical procedures used to manage a spastic upper limb in patients with UMN
syndrome must be individualized and are based on the presence or absence of volitional
muscle control. Because UMN syndrome affects the entire neuromotor unit, including
the joint, all structures must be evaluated and addressed. Various targets for
intervention at the neuromotor units include procedures directed at the innervating
nerve, muscle, musculotendinous junction, or tendon itself. Specific techniques consist
of neurotomy, muscle origin release or slide, myotomy, fractional lengthening at the
musculotendinous junction, tendon Z-lengthening, or tenotomy (Table 2). The technique
that is used is based on the presence (functional) or absence (nonfunctional) of volitional
control within the neuromotor unit.
In addition to surgical treatment options directed at the dysfunctional neuromotor unit;
concomitant pathologies, such as internal joint derangements, heterotopic ossification,
and contracted periarticular soft tissues; and integument must be addressed to fully
correct the joint deformity.
Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Shoulder7,11
(Resource 11)
Spasticity within the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, subscapularis, and teres major muscles
may result in an adduction and internal rotation posture at the glenohumeral joint.
In the functional shoulder, fractional lengthening can be performed to correct the deformity.
In the nonfunctional shoulder, tenotomy may be effective in improving passive shoulder
abduction and external rotation to enhance axillary hygiene and to improve quality of life.

Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Shoulder
The deformity that commonly occurs in the shoulder of patients with UMN syndrome is
adduction and internal rotation. This is attributed to the spasticity of the pectoralis
major, latissimus dorsi, subscapularis, and teres major muscles. Often, increased motor
activity of the posterior deltoid and the long head of the triceps can produce a
hyperextension deformity at the glenohumeral joint. In some patients, an abduction
deformity may be present because of the spasticity within the deltoid and supraspinatus
muscles.
In the functional shoulder, spasticity within the involved muscles can be markedly
reduced or eliminated via fractional lengthening. In the nonfunctional shoulder,
tenotomy can be performed for the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, subscapularis, and
teres major to achieve improved shoulder abduction and external rotation. In certain
patients, paralysis of the rotator cuff muscles may result in painful inferior subluxation
of glenohumeral joint. A proximally based, long head of the biceps suspension tenodesis
can be performed to alleviate the symptomatic inferior subluxation.
Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Elbow7,11
The spastic biceps, brachialis, and BCR muscles can create an elbow flexion deformity in
patients with UMN syndrome.
In the functional elbow, theses muscles can be released from their origin or lengthened at the
musculocutaneous junction to correct the spastic elbow flexion deformity.
For the nonfunctional elbow, the spastic elbow flexors can be transected within the muscle,
divided at the tendon, or denervated with musculocutaneous nerve neurotomy.

Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Elbow
Surgical correction of a flexed elbow deformity should focus on addressing the spastic
BCR, brachialis, and/or biceps motor units. In the functional elbow, these elbow flexors
can be released from their skeletal origin or fractionally lengthened at the
musculotendinous junction to correct the deformity. Specifically, for the distal biceps
tendon, Z-lengthening and fractional lengthening can be performed (Video 1). The goal
of these procedures is to enhance functional ROM while preserving the ability to
perform active or volitional elbow flexion. In the nonfunctional elbow, the spastic or
contracted muscles can be released from their origin, transected through the muscle
(myotomy), or divided at the tendon (tenotomy). In addition, division of the
musculocutaneous nerve (neurotomy) is highly effective at eliminating the neurally
mediated spasticity in the biceps and brachialis muscle of the nonfunctional elbow.
In patient with long-standing spasticity and deformity, elbow joint contractures and the
formation of heterotopic ossification may limit the ability of muscle release alone to
address motion limitations. Therefore, if an elbow flexion contracture of more than 30°
persists despite attempts at muscle release or lengthening, an anterior and/or posterior
compartment capsular release and/or joint débridement may be necessary in addition to
resection of any heterotopic ossification that is limiting motion.

Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Intrinsic Plus Hand
A clenched fist deformity may mask spasticity of the intrinsic muscles, which may require
release, lengthening, tenotomy, or denervation based on the potential for function in the
hand. An intrinsic plus hand, which often may present as a swan-neck deformity, can
result from spasticity or contracture of the interossei and lumbrical muscles12 (Resource
12).
In the functional hand with intrinsic spasticity, the origins of the dorsal and palmar
interossei muscles can be released off the metacarpals via a dorsal approach; they are
then allowed to slide distally and scar in their newly lengthened position or fractional
lengthening can be performed via a palmar approach. However, in the nonfunctional
hand with spastic intrinsic muscles, the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve can be
transected. If the intrinsic muscles are contracted, tenotomy of the lateral bands at the
level of the metacarpal heads should be performed. In patients with joint contractures,
release of the checkrein ligament, metacarpophalangeal joint capsule, and/or collateral
ligaments may be necessary.
Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Thumb7,8
A thumb-in-palm deformity is attributed to spasticity or myostatic contracture within the flexor
pollicis longus and thenar muscles.
Abnormal motor tone in the adductor pollicis may contribute to the thumb-in-palm deformity.
In the functional thumb, flexor pollicis longus fractional or Z-lengthening combined with
thenar origin release may correct the thumb-in-palm deformity.
Within the nonfunctional hand and thumb, the flexor pollicis longus can be tenotomized and
transferred to the en mass superficialis-to-profundus tendons.
Denervation of the adductor pollicis and thenar muscles can be performed in the
nonfunctional thumb to eliminate spasticity.

Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Thumb
Spasticity of the flexor pollicis longus and/or the thenar muscles may result in a thumb-
in-palm deformity, which may be painful, impede grasp, and cause severe hygiene
issues. In the functional hand, lengthening procedures for the flexor pollicis longus can
be performed, but they may unmask spasticity within the flexor pollicis brevis and/or
adductor pollicis muscles, resulting in incomplete correction of the deformity. Therefore,
a thenar muscle slide and release of the adductor pollicis from the third metacarpal via a
palmar approach can be performed.
In a patient with a nonfunctional hand and thumb, the spastic clenched fist and thumb-
in-palm deformity can be corrected via transfer of the flexor pollicis longus to the en
masse superficialis-to-profundus tendons. Specific to the nonfunctional thumb,
neurectomy of the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve and the recurrent motor
branch of the median nerve may eliminate the spastic tone within the adductor pollicis
and thenar muscles to further correct the thumb-in-palm deformity. Extensor pollicis
longus rerouting through the first extensor compartment is an adjunct to correcting a
thumb-in-palm deformity in the functional or nonfunctional thumb by converting the
adduction force of the extensor pollicis longus into an abductor in the radial and palmar
direction.
Techniques/Procedures | Surgical Techniques: Postoperative Management
Early postoperative rehabilitation consists of rehabilitation, stretching, and passive joint ROM.
The ability to perform early active ROM in the functional upper extremity is dependent on the
surgical techniques that were performed.
Orthotics are used immediately to maintain the correction achieved intraoperatively while
minimizing the development of recurrent deformities.

In the acute postoperative setting, rehabilitation is focused on edema management and
stretching of the joints to improve the physiologic arc of motion. Orthotics are used
immediately to maintain the new resting length of the formerly spastic and contracture
pathologic muscles. In the functional upper extremity, early active ROM is encouraged
after it is safe to proceed based on the surgical procedure that was performed. For
example, with fractional lengthening, active ROM can be initiated immediately; however,
with Z-lengthening, active ROM must be performed cautiously to minimize the risk of
tenorrhaphy rupture. In the subacute to late postoperative setting, more aggressive
stretching can be instituted with progression to strengthening exercises if volitional
control is present. Full-time orthotic use can be transitioned to night-time only use as
tolerated to prevent recurrent deformities.
